baseline_description.interaction: Drag each rotary selector to a labeled detent, then Fire.
baseline_description.difficulty: Irregular block boundaries require re-encoding neighboring cells.

rationale.visual: The agent must locate cells within two-dimensional rows and differently sized labeled block spans, count in the bracket's indicated direction, distinguish persistent shot marks, and set labeled detents on a flat selector. Fleet adjacency is horizontal or vertical in the same plane. No depth, viewpoint reconstruction or three-dimensional object relationship is involved.
rationale.temporal: All relevant accumulated evidence remains on the chart: seen cells retain hit/miss/sunk marks, the manifest retains sunk status, and the selectors and sweep count remain visible. A new screenshot supplies everything needed for the next action. Full-mode drags are validated only by their start position, release position and displacement; neither duration nor an evolving target matters. Fire produces its static result synchronously. Thus neither interaction mode requires hidden past-state memory, motion interpretation or timed control.
rationale.reasoning_planning: Not required for the implemented completion condition: the grader passes exactly when every vessel is sunk, with no shot limit or efficiency threshold. Firing at every still-unmarked chart cell is a general legitimate UI solution; each shot only adds persistent coverage and cannot obstruct later shots. Converting the visible location into its explicitly explained band/block/count address is spatial interpretation, not an additional constraint-inference requirement. Inferring possible straight vessels and allocating the two sweeps does constitute reasoning and planning for higher efficiency, but the implementation grades that separately and explicitly allows lower-scoring enumeration passes.
rationale.exploration_interface: The initial chart conceals every vessel's occupancy. FIRE is an active probe at an agent-chosen location, and a sweep probes a selected block; only those actions reveal the corresponding hidden cells. A screenshot-only search therefore acquires relevant fleet information through interaction, even if it searches exhaustively. This is hidden-world exploration rather than learning undocumented controls: the designation rule, drag instruction, sweep behavior and fleet rules are already visible. Fleet truth carried in runtime_fleet is not drawn into unshot cells and is not available to the screenshot-only solver.

source_evidence.claim: Cells are generated in row/column coordinates and assigned band, block and directional count addresses; legal vessels occupy straight horizontal or vertical runs.
The visible chart is a flat SVG with row labels, block brackets and arrows, planar cell marks, and a fleet-length manifest.
Every shot adds cells to m.seen and redraws persistent evidence, sunk status and sweep count immediately; no previous chart information necessary for the next probe disappears.
Simplified mode uses value-button clicks. Full mode uses a stationary knob and release-angle detent selection, with no hold duration, movement-driven simulation or temporal acceptance window.
Full-mode replay checks start/release geometry and detent identity, not elapsed time or an evolving action state.

Shots monotonically extend seen cells. Passing depends only on sinking all vessels. Extra shots reduce efficiency, but there is no shot-count or efficiency pass threshold; enumeration is explicitly permitted by the implementation.
The exported verifier adopts the independent grader's passed flag and efficiency score, without imposing an additional quality threshold.
Visible instructions explain the address mapping and state that fewer shots earn a higher score. The chart marks allow fixed-order enumeration without inferring hidden vessel arrangements.
A fleet cell is drawn as a hit only after it has been shot; unshot cells display neither occupancy nor orientation.
The selected designation determines which hidden cells a shot or sweep reveals, making information acquisition depend on the agent's chosen probes.
Fleet locations are sampled from legal arrangements and are not specified by the initially visible chart geometry.

limitations: The requested task text also encourages using as few shots as possible. This required-capability classification uses the implemented completion criterion, which accepts exhaustive search with a reduced efficiency score. A classification of efficient search performance would include reasoning and planning for vessel constraints and sweep allocation.
No browser gameplay or human-usability check was performed; the findings are based on source inspection.
coordinates_by_another_name.review_scope: Read the first-pass decisions and all rationale/evidence; independently read complete env/task/controls metadata, generator, browser JavaScript/CSS, grader, verifier, solver, and the implementing exported-result loader. No browser or gameplay test was run.

baseline_description.interaction: Hold left/right steering and up/down throttle/brake keys together; release returns that axis to neutral.
baseline_description.difficulty: A third perpendicular approach and shorter yielding horizons couple the turn to three traffic streams.

rationale.visual: Necessary geometry is entirely planar: car position and heading, rectangular vehicle footprints, crossing road corridors, gaps between cars, and full-body containment within the departure rectangle. The town buildings do not introduce depth-dependent navigation or occlusion.
rationale.temporal: Steering continuously changes heading in proportion to current speed, and throttle, brake, or coast continuously change speed. Successful execution requires sustaining and ending these effects during the turn. Traffic also moves and brakes in response to predicted conflicts, so successive visible states support judging safe entry and slowing. A static target click or automatic drive-to-goal control is absent. Persistent simplified buttons retain the same time-extended control requirement.
rationale.reasoning_planning: The agent must choose when and where to enter traffic and a feasible turn trajectory. Acceleration affects later stopping distance and steering progress; an early or late turn can put part of the car over the road boundary, while entering an occupied future path causes collision. The departure side determines which road to enter. These coupled consequences require planning beyond recognizing the yellow car or striped target.
rationale.exploration_interface: The scene, target, no-contact/road constraints, input mappings, speed, and current axis settings are visible. No view-reveal control or hidden rule must be discovered. Driver-specific braking horizons are not displayed, but identifying those parameters through probing is not required: the agent can judge visible motion and gaps, and treat actual braking as ongoing driving feedback. Starting the engine and observing traffic is ordinary task progression, rather than an interaction that uncovers a hidden interface or necessary concealed clue.

source_evidence.claim: The canonical baseline is difficulty 4 and full interaction.
Rendering uses a top-down canvas with planar rotated cars, visible cross-shaped roads, and a striped destination; all traffic bodies are drawn.
Spatial success and failure use 2D rotated rectangles, road-boundary intersections, and containment of every car corner in the goal.

The browser advances fixed physical ticks with responsive moving traffic and integrates speed, heading, and position; held keys or latched buttons continue affecting the drive until their controls change.
The grader replays ongoing control effects and traffic motion, validates each tick and mode-specific control source, and requires physical arrival. Merely claiming a final win does not pass.

Predicted relative-motion conflicts alter traffic braking, current pedal choice changes later speed, steering changes later trajectory, and collision or road departure terminates the attempt. These dependencies constrain safe entry and turning decisions.
Seeds vary departure side and traffic phases, speeds, and braking response, while the goal and road layout impose a left or right driving route.

The initial render displays the entire relevant road scene and destination, draws traffic and brake lights, states the mission and yielding caution, labels the controls, and displays speed and selected axes. Driving feedback updates these visible quantities without an information-reveal mechanic.

Accepted transcripts consist of start, mode-specific driving controls, physical ticks, and submit. No discovery, probing, learned-rule response, or hidden-information retrieval is required for success.

All five profiles were examined: D1-D2 allow right turns with one or two slower traffic streams; D3 allows either turn and three cars per stream; D4-D5 use three streams with shorter braking horizons and narrower roads. Both implemented interaction modes control steering and pedal axes. These variations do not remove planar navigation, sustained control, or route/traffic decisions and do not add an information-reveal requirement.
Every profile supplies traffic and road parameters to the same generator and physical model. Interaction selection does not change the generated spatial world.
Exported verification loads the submitted result, truth, and public state, then applies the independent Courtesy Junction physical replay grader.

The test solver reads private world and simulation state and predicts candidate continuations. Its success is not evidence that a screenshot-only agent sees driver parameters or must use this privileged strategy.

baseline_description.interaction: Click the intended adjacent ceramic tile directly on the crossing.
baseline_description.difficulty: The baseline keeps three shuffled lifetimes and three lanterns, then hides the crack stages of two revisited core tiles so their ages must be retained across decisions.

rationale.visual: The necessary spatial model is a planar row-and-column graph: identify adjacent tiles, gaps, glaze colours, lantern locations, and the exit. The slight CSS perspective and raised ceramic decoration do not require reconstructing depth, occlusion geometry, or a three-dimensional route.
rationale.temporal: The colour-to-lifetime mapping is shuffled and is not printed in the normal UI. Learning it requires relating a tile's earlier departure to its later crack or collapse state across accepted moves. Later revisits depend on elapsed move count since first departure; the visible crack stages are qualitative rather than exact ages. D1 and D2 remove gallery tiles but retain shuffled lifetimes and their opening observations. D3-D5 add gallery crack masking. Both interaction modes use the same discrete movement progression, so neither removes this provisional temporal requirement. This does not require a continuous stream during an otherwise passive observation period.
rationale.reasoning_planning: The agent must choose the collection order and route through a cyclic floor while preserving usable return paths. Leaving a tile starts a fuse that never resets on revisiting, so a locally legal move can make a later required crossing fail. The generator constructs a feasible route and rejects several geometry-only policies that expire, while the grader independently checks each departure age and requires all lanterns before the exit can pass. The same dependency is active at every difficulty; profile changes alter floor size, lantern count, glaze lifetimes, and masking rather than removing route planning.
rationale.exploration_interface: The agent must learn an unknown task response through interaction: which glaze colour survives how many subsequent moves. The initial board and normal rendered controls provide no numerical lifetime legend. Moving through the opening corridor supplies observations from which the rule mapping must be inferred and then applied to later route decisions. This is learning the behaviour of the floor, beyond recognizing explicit movement controls or receiving an already interpreted next instruction. Every profile preserves the shuffled mapping and calibration corridor, and both input modes reveal it through the same movement effects. The developer cheat panel and the scripted solver's state-file access are outside a normal screenshot-only solution.

source_evidence.claim: Tiles are placed by row and column and visibly encode glaze, gallery cover, walker, lantern collection, start, and door; full mode makes those same tiles the click targets.
The board remains a two-dimensional CSS grid; the two-degree perspective tilt is presentational.
The grader requires symmetric orthogonal adjacency at Manhattan distance one, with no depth coordinate.
The active difficulty supplies distinct fuse lengths, which are shuffled among the visible glaze colours for each generated challenge.
Tile stages depend on the difference between current move count and first departure, with qualitative stages ending at critical and shattered rather than a visible numerical countdown.
Each adjacent movement increments the step, records only the first departure, updates all shattered tiles, and fails if the destination has expired before collecting any destination lantern.

Generation evaluates revisit gaps, assigns fuses that preserve an intended route, and accepts the assignment only when the configured number of sampled geometry-only routes fail. This establishes concrete route-and-fuse dependencies without proving all alternative routes impossible.
The independent replay enforces orthogonal movement, the selected input surface, persistent first-departure ages, expired-destination failure, and collecting the full lantern set before exiting.
Exported verification reloads the result and independently invokes the same movement-replay grader; it does not accept a completion flag by itself.
The opening corridor supplies a walk before the generated core; movement through it is required to reach the objective region.
The first calibration tiles deliberately contain every active glaze in shuffled order, enabling learning from the observable consequences of walking away.
The normal render contains the objective, board, optional directional buttons, and pass/fail readout, but no displayed fuse mapping or interpreted calibration results.
The developer answer-reveal panel is gated by cheat mode in the query string and is absent from normal play.

The scripted solver reads public and ground-truth files and takes the certified route directly; this bypasses the screenshot agent's need to learn the glaze mapping and is not capability evidence for a visible solution.

The canonical baseline is D3/full. All five profiles keep multiple fuse lengths; D1-D2 have no galleries and D3-D5 have two, four, and six. The two input modes change only direct tile clicks versus directional buttons.

Gallery cover suppresses the crack strokes, but the separate stage rules still change brightness, position, and disappearance. The implementation therefore does not support treating every gallery stage as completely visually hidden.

limitations: This is source-based classification, with no isolated browser gameplay verification. Gallery styling hides crack lines but retains other stage cues; their practical visibility through the shadow has not been assessed in rendered screenshots. The temporal decision relies on learning the shuffled lifetimes and reasoning about move ages rather than assuming complete gallery-state concealment.

The generator checks a bounded collection of geometry-only paths and a pair of routes whose success changes when the glaze mapping changes. These are not an exhaustive proof that every individual generated board requires learning the mapping or revisiting a gallery tile. The configuration-wide temporal audit remains deferred; no supported general solution that ignores change and prior state was established in this first pass.

baseline_description.interaction: Drag directly from vertex to vertex to lay a connected run of loop edges; right-click a visible edge to toggle an exclusion mark.
baseline_description.difficulty: The baseline uses thirteen hat tiles, nine or fewer retained clues, and a loop that must cross at least five internal tile boundaries.

rationale.visual: The necessary geometry is planar: match a number to its irregular hat-shaped face, distinguish its atomic boundary segments and junctions, and follow shared edges and connectivity. The board is a 2D SVG graph with x/y vertices; no depth, occlusion ordering, or 3D transformation is needed.
rationale.temporal: The entire graph, all retained clues, and the current loop/exclusion marks persist. A general solution can reason from the current static board and enter each edge as an independent drag between fixed neighboring dots. Full-mode validation checks spatial path contiguity, travel distance, and sample count; it checks no elapsed duration, speed, release window, or evolving world state. There is no need to remember a vanished clue or interpret motion. Simplified mode likewise uses untimed edge selection and mark buttons.
rationale.reasoning_planning: Each chosen shared edge contributes to the counts of its incident faces and changes which other edges can be selected without branching, making a dead end, or closing a separate loop. Solving therefore requires combining local numeric constraints with global cycle connectivity. The generator retains clues only when these public constraints uniquely determine its solution, and the grader requires that exact loop. These are dependencies beyond identifying or tracing visible shapes.
rationale.exploration_interface: The retained clues and complete boundary graph are drawn immediately and remain available. Missing clues are omitted constraints, not information that can be uncovered by probing. The task instructions specify the loop rules and both input surfaces. Dragging, selecting, marking, resetting, and certification operate on already visible information; none is required to reveal a clue or learn an unknown rule. Optional mark feedback or a failed certification does not establish a necessary exploration demand. The private-state solver's ground-truth access is not part of this visible solution.

source_evidence.claim: Builds a planar normalized graph of x/y vertices, atomic shared edges, polygonal faces, and interior label points; these are the spatial relationships needed for grounding the clues.
Renders the actual face polygons, clue numbers, straight boundary segments, marked loop edges, exclusions, and visible junction dots together in one 2D SVG board.

Full mode accepts a stroke across any adjacent pair of fixed vertices, including a single edge, and commits on pointerup. Simplified mode selects an edge and applies a stationary mark button. Neither input path uses a clock or automatically moving geometry.

The direct-stroke contract requires contiguous edges, matching endpoints, enough pointer samples, and at least 70 percent of the geometric path length in travel. It has no timestamp, duration, speed, or timed-release constraint, so static dot-to-dot drags suffice.
Each board render retains all clues and redraws every current loop and exclusion mark, allowing decisions from present visible state instead of a hidden history.
The implemented solution constraints couple face counts, vertex degrees, and connected-cycle closure; satisfying one clue constrains subsequent edge choices at neighboring faces and vertices.

Generates a nontrivial loop, calculates face counts, and removes clues only if the remaining visible clue set still has exactly one solution; rejects instances that do not meet the requested clue profile.
Replays the selected interaction surface and accepts only the exact final solution edge set, so arbitrary shape tracing or merely producing any closed curve cannot pass.
The exported verifier independently reruns this same grader against the exported result, ground truth, and public state, preserving the exact loop contract.
The provided task description states the exact-count and nonbranching loop rules, dot-to-dot dragging/right-click marking in Full, edge selection/mark controls in Simplified, and certification.

All retained clues appear in the initial board. Selecting and marking only alter focus or recorded edge marks; there is no hidden clue-reveal step or unknown interface mapping needed to infer the loop.

The scripted solver loads ground_truth.json and orders the private solution edge IDs. This demonstrates a wiring strategy, not information available to a screenshot-only player, and is excluded from the classification.

The canonical baseline is difficulty 3/Full. Reviewed all five profiles and both input modes: tile counts are 6, 9, 13, 17, and 22; clue fractions are 0.92, 0.8, 0.68, 0.58, and 0.5; minimum internal solution edges are 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9. These parameters vary the static graph and constraints while preserving the same four capability labels in all ten configurations.

Every difficulty uses the same parameterized static puzzle construction. Interaction is carried as a condition without changing the generated geometry, clues, or solution; no difficulty introduces motion, hidden past information, or an action-duration rule.

baseline_description.interaction: Hold/release the left or right key or motor pad; release returns to neutral.
baseline_description.difficulty: Baseline: infer both angular velocities and build a crest one link above the passive pivot.

rationale.visual: The necessary geometry is planar: the shoulder pivot, elbow, free tip, relative link angles, and vertical separation from a horizontal target line. The renderer maps both link angles directly into an SVG plane, and the grader uses the same planar tip-height formula. Brass shading and offset-arm decoration introduce no depth decision.
rationale.temporal: The current drawing shows positions but does not display the two angular velocities. Successful swing control uses changes in arm pose and chooses how long torque remains active and when it reverses or becomes neutral. Full mode explicitly holds torque until release; simplified mode retains torque between clicks while the same physical state evolves. Automatic success capture removes any need to time submission, but it does not remove the preceding swing-control demand. All five profiles retain this mechanism; only target height and torque strength change. A numerical check of one generated seed found that leaving any one of the three torque states unchanged for the entire trial failed at every difficulty, including D1, so a single latched command is not a general solution.
rationale.reasoning_planning: Only the elbow is actuated, while the shoulder responds through the coupled two-link dynamics. A torque choice affects both later orientation and momentum: the agent must use elbow motion to build the later shoulder swing and place the two links into a sufficiently high crest. Recognizing the current tip height alone does not determine a useful control interval. This action dependency persists across the target-height and torque profiles and both input modes.
rationale.exploration_interface: The goal line, arm geometry, passive-pivot label, torque direction controls, active torque readout, and held-versus-latched instructions are visible. There is no hidden panel, undisclosed control mapping, or information-reveal action required before solving. Observing the arms respond while controlling the swing is ordinary control feedback. Exact seeded mass and velocity values used by the supplied privileged solver are not visible, but a screenshot-based feedback solution can estimate motion without inspecting or discovering those numerical values.

source_evidence.claim: The scene draws a horizontal goal line and two links in one SVG plane; the elbow and tip positions are calculated directly from the two planar angles.
Acceptance depends on the same two-link planar height, not perspective, depth ordering, or a hidden third dimension.

Positions and velocities evolve under signed torque. The UI displays arm poses rather than velocities, full-mode release returns to neutral, and simplified clicks latch the selected torque while integration continues.
The first height crossing automatically ends the simulation and leaves a persistent success message for later submission, so submission timing is not the temporal requirement.

The baseline is D4/full. D1-D5 set target heights -0.5, 0, 0.6, 1.0, and 1.6 and torques 2.5, 2.0, 1.8, 1.5, and 1.2, with time_scale 0.5 throughout. The two interfaces change holding versus latching rather than the dynamics or available torque states.

The coupled mass-matrix equations apply motor torque only to the elbow and carry both velocities into future states; grading replays the timed torque transitions and requires an actual height crossing. Earlier torque choices therefore determine the later attainable crest.

Every profile uses the same two-link physical system, seeded small initial angles and velocities, and seeded second-link mass. The profile changes active target height and torque parameters without adding a direct position-control or automatic swing-up route.

The initial interface exposes the entire arm configuration, goal, passive shoulder, signed torque pads, Start and Submit controls, and explicit input-mode instructions; the active torque remains visible during operation.

The supplied solver reads numerical physics and simulation pose directly and computes energy feedback and predicted crests. Those reads are privileged wiring evidence, not visible information or evidence that screenshot solvers must use hidden-state access.
The exported verifier reloads the independent physical grader and submits exported events, truth, and public state for replay rather than accepting the browser's success flag alone.

limitations: No screenshot-only or isolated browser gameplay run was performed. The visible solution describes the control demands established by source; the privileged solver does not establish human or screenshot-agent success across seeds. Temporal labels remain provisional pending the dedicated configuration-wide temporal audit.

baseline_description.interaction: Choose hammer mode and direction, click an exposed top face, and use transfer/orbit buttons.
baseline_description.difficulty: A raised socket and thin cutting edge require choosing between flattening and raising material; two excess voxels may be split.

rationale.visual: The agent must recover occupied positions and vertical column heights from projected voxel faces and compare the full solid with a target containing a hole and several heights. Neighbor height determines whether draw or upset is legal. The top view deliberately drops the height coordinate and cannot by itself distinguish correct thickness, so the perspective is task information rather than decoration.
rationale.temporal: A solution can use the current solid, persistent target, selected tool and direction, and current heat indicator. Geometry changes only on discrete strikes and remains inspectable; orbit is a discrete view change rather than motion that must be interpreted. Cold strikes do not alter the solid, reheating preserves it, and heating saturates at full heat. The agent can wait for that visible capped state and resume; it does not need an elapsed-duration estimate, a changing trajectory, a disappearing clue, or a timed hold. Both input modes commit discrete actions, and full-mode drags have endpoint or displacement checks without duration requirements. Camera inspection concerns the persistent present solid rather than a transient earlier event.
rationale.reasoning_planning: Each transfer decreases one column and increases another, changing which later transfers are legal. The agent must choose between lowering, raising, and permanently discarding material while respecting neighbor equality/inequality, the height cap, and the target's complete volume. A locally convenient split can leave insufficient metal; routing can require intermediate changes to columns that are already useful. This is a constrained material-rearrangement problem, including at the two easier profiles.
rationale.exploration_interface: The baseline's three-layer workpiece can contain entirely occluded columns in its initial projection. The normal UI solution must use orbit to expose relevant current geometry; the target turns with it. Top view reveals occupancy and accessible contact faces but discards height, so it does not replace inspection of the solid. The tool meanings themselves are explicitly displayed: the exploration requirement comes from revealing geometry, not from guessing controls or treating strike feedback as exploration. Profiles 4 and 5 retain this requirement; profiles 1 and 2 have the exception below.

configuration_exceptions.reason: These profiles cap every column at two layers and use a one-layer target without socket relief. In the implemented initial projection, a one-layer top retains an exposed upper patch even behind surrounding two-layer columns; the higher tops are also exposed. Thus the current column information and complete flat target can be read from the initial view without an information-revealing orbit or probing action. The visible tool descriptions suffice in both modes. Heights and constrained redistribution still require 3D visual understanding and reasoning/planning.

source_evidence.claim: Both easier profiles set max_height to 2 and relief to false.
Without relief all target columns are one layer, and initial surplus respects the height cap; subsequent moves also enforce that cap.
The fixed initial projection and voxel face geometry leave an exposed top patch when maximum height difference is one. Both interfaces present the same solid and explicit mode/direction rules.
Baseline generation constructs multiple target column heights, a through-eye, and a raised voxel, then rotates the actual height field.
Oblique projection encodes z, renders individual stacked voxel faces, and changes the facing sides with orbit; the top-view branch omits z.
Independent replay enforces transfers between column heights and accepts only exact equality of the full height arrays, not the silhouette.
Heat is capped in the forge; transfers preserve heights, cold strikes are no-ops, and successful material changes happen discretely at strike.
Every repaint displays the current workpiece and persistent target, current heat category and meter, selected tool and direction, and discard/reheat ledger.
Simplified actions use clicks; full drags commit on pointer release using the contact point, transfer rectangle, or orbit displacement, without a hold-time or motion-tracking rule.
Draw and upset use different source/destination height constraints and both conserve material; split irreversibly removes one unit.

Initial states are built through interacting reversible redistributions plus a finite surplus; reversing the generated route is a private wiring witness, not information supplied to the screenshot agent.
The grader replays each changing column constraint, verifies conservation including discarded material, and requires the resulting solid to equal the target.

Orbit changes the actual projection. Painter ordering permits tall columns to occlude lower ones, and hit testing accepts only currently exposed top faces. Inspection can therefore reveal geometry unavailable in the original screenshot.
The UI explicitly shows tool rules and view controls and states that target and workpiece turn together. Simplified orbit buttons and the full orbit rail expose the same views.

The wiring solver reads the private generated solution and uses top-view coordinates for contact. Its success would not establish that height information is visible in top view or that screenshot agents can avoid planning and inspection.

ember_anvil.review_scope: Read all returned first-pass decisions, rationales, source evidence, profile exceptions, and source-geometry diagnostic results and limitations. This primary check is a rationale review, not an independent complete-source annotation or gameplay test.

baseline_description.interaction: Select a material and paint directly on the canvas with a pointer drag. The browser records the stroke path and the grader replays its rasterized effect.
baseline_description.difficulty: The reference configuration: three connected target patches, two fire sources, three oil pockets, a one-cell brush, eroding gates, and a visible hot branch.

rationale.visual: The necessary geometry is a flat grid: distinguish oil, fire, marked plants, and ordinary plant links; locate their four-neighbour connections; and place the brush so the oil branches are disconnected without cutting the target route. Neither rendering nor propagation requires depth or three-dimensional relationships.
rationale.temporal: A static firebreak strategy avoids a necessary temporal relationship. Stone replaces ordinary plant cells immediately. When heated stone later erodes, it becomes empty space rather than restoring the plant. Fire spreads only into adjacent plant cells, so an initially cut link stays noncombustible. The visible hot branch is ordinary non-target plant and can also be cut before its flame reaches oil. Subsequent burning can run automatically until the visible final condition is reached; it does not require tracking motion, remembering a hidden state, or sustaining an input. Full mode permits isolated taps with no duration threshold. The need to place initial barriers before oil ignites is an initial action deadline, which does not alone establish this capability. All five profiles retain this static alternative in both interfaces.
rationale.reasoning_planning: The intervention must preserve propagation through the marked patches while disconnecting the oil hazards. Choosing stone cuts near oil rather than extinguishing the main connected fire route uses the causal consequences of material placement for the later burn outcome. That fire-containment decision goes beyond recognizing or matching a displayed object.
rationale.exploration_interface: The initial rendering exposes the complete plant/oil layout, marks the gates and target cells, and displays the material palette and the applicable painting or coordinate-stamp controls. There is no hidden region, concealed target fact, or interface rule that must be revealed by a preliminary probe. A normal solution can infer a firebreak from the visible material and connection layout; observing paint feedback or the automatic burn does not by itself add exploration. The supplied solver's direct model/truth reads are not treated as screenshot access.

source_evidence.claim: Every cell is drawn as a rectangle in the two-dimensional field. Colour identifies materials, cyan rings identify gates, and gold outlines identify unconsumed target plants.
The world consists of a connected plant route, marked patches, off-route oil spurs, and a visible non-target bypass branch, all expressed in X/Y grid coordinates.

Stone can overwrite non-target plant cells. Fire spreads only to cells currently containing plant, and stone erosion produces empty cells. Consequently preemptive cuts remain noncombustible after erosion, so repairing gates is not intrinsically necessary.
The extra oil-heating branch is rendered plant material outside target cells. It is not protected from stone painting and can be severed from the initial visible layout.
Simplified mode performs a single immediate stamp; full mode paints on pointerdown and additional movement. A stationary pointerdown/up placement has no minimum hold duration or motion requirement.

Independent replay implements the same irreversible plant removal and empty-cell erosion. It accepts either surface's legitimate single-point brushes and grades burned targets plus absence of oil ignition, without requiring adaptive water use, gate repair, or prolonged input.

Material placement can stop flame or remove combustible links; flame must still reach every target, while any accumulated oil ignition fails. Placement choices therefore have competing causal consequences for the later outcome.

The canvas renders the whole current field without an interaction-gated reveal. Visible instructions identify the goal, material buttons, direct painting or coordinate stamping, and the meaning of gate and target rings.

The supplied solver reads ground truth and model state to choose gate repairs and cooling actions. This is one adaptive implementation strategy, not evidence that every visible-UI solution must be temporal.

baseline_description.interaction: Click an open hex cell to place one stake directly.
baseline_description.difficulty: The unchanged baseline seven-cell-diameter field leaves several interacting escape branches. Exhaustive search certifies a three- to five-placement shortest win. A newly revealed wind order changes later route ties.

rationale.visual: The solution requires reading adjacency and connectivity in an axial hex field, distinguishing barriers, the fox, open cells, and the boundary, and grounding a chosen barrier location. These are planar relationships. The fox and fence illustrations do not introduce depth or a third spatial coordinate. All five difficulties retain this geometry.
rationale.temporal: In the simplified baseline, the fox moves only after an accepted placement and the new position remains visible. Every placed barrier persists, the remaining budget is displayed, and the new wind order remains on the panel. The next decision can therefore be made from a settled current screenshot without interpreting motion, comparing old and new winds, remembering an earlier hidden board state, or sustaining an action. Unrevealed future wind is future information, not relevant hidden earlier state. The automatic move and updated vane alone do not establish temporal understanding. This also applies to simplified difficulties 1 through 5; full interaction has the exception below.
rationale.reasoning_planning: A placement permanently removes a cell from the escape graph and immediately triggers a shortest-route fox reply. A useful action must account for the resulting route, later barrier opportunities, rim escape, and the limited stake budget. Recognition of an open hex alone is insufficient. Even the easier profiles retain the constraint of cutting all paths rather than selecting a marked answer; the larger profiles retain the same action dependencies. Wind rank is compared before onward options and degree, and gives each neighboring direction a unique priority, so the classification does not credit those later sort terms as extra necessary reasoning.
rationale.exploration_interface: The prompt explains placement, the fox policy, the changing visible wind, and the enclosure goal. The board, fox, budget, and current wind are directly shown. Placing a stake produces the next task state and automatically supplies the next wind; no separate probe, hidden-information inspection, or learning of an unspecified interface rule is required. Full interaction likewise explicitly instructs the hold, numbered marks, return, and release; the driver marks are supplied during that routine instructed placement transition rather than requiring exploratory discovery.

configuration_exceptions.reason: Every full-mode placement requires an uninterrupted held pointer gesture. The pointer must remain held over a candidate until the driver arms after a 90 ms timer, stay held while the generated numbered marks are visited, and be released only after returning to center. The duration and continuation of the action are necessary even though the revealed marks are static and explicitly numbered. This is temporal control under the current guideline, and is not observation-only temporal demand.

source_evidence.claim: Pointerdown creates a held drag; the 90 ms arming timer checks that the drag still exists over its candidate, movements advance the driver marks, and release fails unless the driver has completed and the pointer is at center.
The full gesture transcript must contain adequate drag geometry and an ordered path through the generated marks followed by the center.
Full-mode transcripts require stake_driver events and gesture validation, so simplified cell clicks cannot substitute for the held gesture.
Browser timeouts, including the driver's arming delay, are scheduled against the shared task clock. Pausing the world does not remove the required held interaction sequence.
Axial q/r cells are projected directly to planar x/y positions; visible cell classes distinguish the rim and existing/player barriers.
Hex polygons, rim coloring, and persistent fence pieces render the spatial distinctions needed for route tracing.
The fox is positioned at its resulting cell, and the panels display the current stake count, placement count, and complete current wind order.

A click adds a persistent fence, computes one fox reply, and automatically finishes that turn; the updated static board and wind support the next choice. No duration or motion interpretation is required by simplified placement.
Escape is graph connectivity to rim cells. The fox selects among open neighbors by shortest rim distance and current wind priority, making barrier consequences predictable from visible current state.
The grader replays each permanent placement and fox reply, rejects occupied placements or incorrect interaction surfaces, enforces the stake budget, and passes only a completed trapped state.
Exported verification loads the submitted result, truth, and public state and delegates to the same independent replay grader; a client completion claim alone does not establish success.
Both interaction modes receive explicit visible input instructions along with the fox movement policy, wind update rule, and goal.
The rendered UI includes the complete prompt, stake count, current wind, full field, fox, and check button, without an information-reveal control needed before planning.

The full-mode driver automatically displays both numbered marks and explicit progress/release instructions once the instructed placement gesture arms it. This is a routine supplied next state, not an unspecified interface rule to discover.
The canonical baseline is difficulty 3 simplified. Profiles 1-5 vary radius, initial fences, plan bounds, and budget; both input modes retain the same enclosure decision problem.

limitations: No gameplay was performed. The bundled solver reads ground_truth.canonical_plan (solver lines 160-170), and the generator searches using the entire future wind sequence (generator lines 159-249 and 322-384). baseline_description.interaction: Arrow keys or WASD move and climb; Shift extinguishes in the current facing direction. The eye and certification buttons remain visible controls.
baseline_description.difficulty: The baseline: a six-floor, nine-cell, two-face tower with a four-canister budget, alternate ladders, three seam crossings, three off-route embers and masonry clutter; route choices have different fire costs.

rationale.visual: The task needs cell adjacency, horizontal seam connections, ladder alignment between floors, and obstruction locations on two flat elevations. The face index changes which planar map is displayed; no depth, 3D orientation or perspective reconstruction is required.
rationale.temporal: The two relevant maps are never displayed together. Route selection and execution across them require retaining previously viewed connections and obstacles while that face is hidden; when inspecting away from the firefighter, its cell is also hidden, and the HUD gives floor and face but no horizontal coordinate. The view stays selected across moves and only the eye changes inspectionFace. This is provisional evidence for hidden earlier-state memory, not a motion or action-duration requirement. The grid changes only through discrete actions, stock and facing persist visibly, and keyboard repeats are ignored.
rationale.reasoning_planning: Ladder and seam choices determine which floor segments are reachable and how many fires must be cleared. Clearing a fire permanently spends one canister, so clearing an unnecessary fire can remove the budget needed later. The generator reserves a one-fire alternative, places other fires away from that route, and protects a canonical route using the nominal stock; the agent must infer an affordable path from visible geometry, not identify a visually distinguished correct fire. The grader accepts any legal route reaching the resident within stock, so neither the generated canonical route nor its three seam crossings is a required action quota.
rationale.exploration_interface: The initial render reveals only the north face, while the L4 resident is on the south face. The eye is a deliberate inspection action revealing a different map without moving the firefighter. This exposes relevant route and goal information that ordinary movement does not automatically reveal, since movement leaves the selected inspection face unchanged. The label rests on this active information acquisition, not on learning keyboard labels or on generic movement feedback. The grader imposes no inspection quota.

configuration_exceptions.reason: With zero seam crossings, one ladder per landing, no walls or decoys, and one route fire, an affordable north-face route to the north-face resident is visible throughout. The agent can leave the initial map selected, move toward each visible upward ladder, clear the single blocking fire and reach the visible resident. Player, stock, facing and cleared fire remain displayed, so hidden-map memory, motion interpretation and timed control can all be avoided.

source_evidence.claim: L1 selects the stated geometry, one canister and zero seam crossings in both interaction modes.
Without seam flips, the protected route and resident stay on face 0; the canonical route clears exactly one fire and requires no inspection.
Leaving the initial face selected keeps the player and all relevant north-face geometry visible; both input modes implement discrete actions.

configuration_exceptions.reason: A simpler general visible solution stays on the north face and follows its sole upward ladder on each floor. With no walls, no decoys, a single required fire and exactly one available canister, this route requires no comparison of competing passages or allocation of resources between later choices. Approaching each visible ladder and clearing the one obstruction is direct visual navigation; the optional alternate-face route need not be considered.

source_evidence.claim: L1 has one ladder per floor, no masonry or decoys, one route fire and no canonical seam changes.
The single-face ascent is preserved and its sole blocking fire consumes the entire one-canister budget, making other routes optional.
Reaching the resident suffices; no alternate-route search, seam or inspection quota is imposed.

configuration_exceptions.reason: The initial north-face map already contains the resident and a complete affordable ladder route. The eye may reveal an optional alternative, but no reveal or experiment is needed before following the visible north-face route.

source_evidence.claim: With L1's zero seam crossings, the resident and route remain on the start face and the generated route has no INSPECT action.
The entire start-face elevation, including ladders, fire, player and resident, is drawn initially.
An inspection count is reported but is not a success condition.

Movement uses planar cell coordinates, ladder connections and edge-to-edge face changes; rendering draws one elevation as rows of numbered cells with wall, ladder, fire, resident and firefighter marks.
The visible geometry is a two-dimensional grid with distinct cell occupants and obstructions, with no depth-dependent spatial mechanic.

Only inspectionFace is drawn. The firefighter is drawn only on that face, the HUD omits x, the eye replaces the view with the face opposite the player, and movement does not restore or follow the view. Prior map and position information therefore disappears from the current screenshot. Actions are discrete and repeated keydown events are ignored.

Generation constructs ladders and seam routes, places fires across a ladder boundary, preserves a one-fire alternative while placing additional fires outside it, and adds walls and decoys subject to route preservation. These create route-dependent fire costs rather than a required extinguishing count.

Replay enforces walls, active fires, ladders, facing and consumable stock. Success is reaching the resident through legal actions with nonnegative stock; it does not require the canonical route, a particular seam count, or exhausting the inventory.

The initial face is the start face; the explicitly bound eye action changes inspectionFace and reveals another complete elevation. No MOVE branch changes inspectionFace, so inspection is active discovery of task information rather than an automatic next-stage reveal.

The player starts on face 0; each configured seam crossing flips faces before the next ascent. L4's three crossings put the resident on face 1, whose goal information is absent from the initial displayed face.
The exported verifier loads the exported result and invokes the same independent replay grader; it adds no hidden canonical-route requirement that would change the visible solution.
The supplied solver reads ground_truth.json and executes solution_actions. Its success cannot establish a screenshot-only solution without map memory or inspection.

limitations: Source-only audit: no rendered browser play or screenshot-only gameplay was performed. Temporal labels remain provisional pending the dedicated configuration-wide temporal audit.

All five difficulty profiles and both interaction profiles were examined. Beyond L1's simpler visible route, no further supported capability exception was established. Levels 2-5 change map size, ladder alternatives, fire stock, obstructions and seam layout; full and simplified modes preserve the same maps and action effects. Some individual seeds may permit an easier route than a configuration-wide solution.

The eye is implemented as selecting the face opposite the firefighter, not toggling the displayed map, and movement leaves that selection unchanged. The visible-solution and memory analysis use this actual behavior; its usability was not verified by gameplay.

baseline_description.interaction: Click the moving token itself, hold the requested physical pad, flick from the indicated token with a real pointer drag, tap relation targets on the stage, and drag cargo into the live bay.
baseline_description.difficulty: The baseline: six competing tokens, relation-based relay instructions, predictive moving-target capture, a synchronized hold/release, orientation-gated flicking, and a timed shutter drop under five fresh five-second orders.

rationale.visual: The required geometry is planar: token centers relative to a vertical gate, needle positions relative to a notch, compass orientation and drag direction, down-left token placement, matching surface marks, and cargo/bay positions. The CSS draws and places these elements on one 820-by-390 logical plane; decorative shadows do not require depth reconstruction.
rationale.temporal: The baseline synchronization dispatch requires a press near the generated start cue and a release near the later amber cue, including at least 310 ms of sustained input. Other dispatches require acting during moving-gate, rotating-pointer, or shutter-opening states. These relationships affect action execution beyond the five-second deadline itself. Both interaction modes preserve these timing predicates. The relay's two visible instructions and persistent first-tap feedback do not independently require temporal memory.
rationale.reasoning_planning: A general solution follows the complete stated order and matches its visual conditions. The baseline relay's down-left relation is 2D spatial grounding, and its second line explicitly names the mark to match; after the first tap, that token is visibly dimmed, leaving the other matching token. There is no hidden rule to infer, alternative action plan to compare, or choice that changes a later dispatch's problem. Flick and cargo actions similarly have their target, direction or destination, and release condition explicitly supplied. The required spatial matching and timed control do not by themselves establish a separate reasoning-and-planning demand.
rationale.exploration_interface: The page shows both order lines, tokens and marks, moving cues, and a direct-control instruction card before action. Simplified mode instead displays labelled stationary controls. No probe or reveal action is necessary to obtain the task rule or relevant token information. A successful dispatch automatically advances to a new fully displayed order, while a relay tap merely dims the accepted token; these are routine progress and feedback. Waiting for an opening or cue reveals an evolving state automatically, not through exploratory interaction.

source_evidence.claim: Coordinates, token motion, pointer rotation and shutter state are computed in a two-dimensional logical stage.
Tokens, visible pattern marks, gate, needles, compass pointers and receiving bays are drawn as positioned planar elements.

The canonical baseline is difficulty 4/full. Its hold duration is 610 ms with 150 ms start/end tolerance, and both input surfaces preserve the dynamic world and timing conditions. All five parameter profiles retain all dispatch families.

Replay requires tagging during a gate crossing, validates both ends and the duration of a hold, and requires the flick release to fall within the requested rotating orientation sector in both modes. The baseline hold minimum is 610 minus twice 150, or 310 ms.
Cargo succeeds only when its release or proxy drop occurs during the receiving bay's opening; full mode additionally checks the actual start and end geometry.

Both direct and proxy holds record pointer-down and pointer-up separately. Animation exposes moving tokens, synchronization start/release cues, pointer headings and shutter openings; these cues determine when inputs succeed.

The relay uses a uniquely identified explicit spatial relation for the first target and an explicitly named visual mark for the second. Difficulty changes direct identification to left/down-left/45-degree relations, but does not add a hidden rule or a branching state dependency.

Gate, hold and flick instructions explicitly give target identity and the condition for acting. Difficulty 5 changes the flick direction to the opposite of the named heading, a planar direction transformation rather than a new action-planning problem.
Rounds reset local interaction state and advance through a pre-generated deck; successful choices do not alter subsequent dispatch problems.
An accepted relay first tap is visibly marked on both the stage and proxy control. Its persistent feedback supports choosing the other marked token without a hidden earlier-state dependency.

The initial round display renders all token visuals, both instruction lines, relevant stage cues, and either explicit direct-action guidance or labelled proxy controls. There is no required information-reveal interaction.
The next dispatch is automatically rendered following a pass, so the transition is routine progression rather than exploration.
The exported verifier invokes the same independent grader on the exported result, ground truth and public state; it does not replace timing and geometry checks with the browser's displayed verdict.

baseline_description.interaction: Hover or focus each mouth to inspect its concealed inlet, then click a mouth to release the next marble.
baseline_description.difficulty: The baseline requires remembering four individually inspected inlet routes, then guiding them through fifteen visible vanes in three coupled rows to a target at exact drop depth seven.

rationale.visual: The task requires matching left/right vane orientations between two 2D lattices and following the connections between adjacent rows, including the currently inspected chute-to-first-row route. The cabinet shading and brass marble do not introduce a depth variable or a 3D spatial problem.
rationale.temporal: The moving marble is an automatic, input-locked transition to another fully visible static board. Its completed path disappears, but all resulting vane states remain visible, as do the target and remaining budget. A general baseline solution can plan over first-row entry columns, inspect only the next entry's chute and click with that inspection still visible; it can recompute from the resulting board rather than remember earlier inlet inspections or drops. Consequently the transient-path presentation and one-at-a-time inlet display do not establish necessary temporal memory. This is a provisional baseline classification; the full-mode inspection-to-drag handoff is called out separately for the later temporal audit.
rationale.reasoning_planning: A chute choice flips one gate in every row and changes which lower gates later marbles visit. The agent must choose the numbers of marbles delivered to different entries so that all vane states match simultaneously before the tray runs out. Matching a currently wrong top vane without considering lower rows can spoil other required states. The final action operators commute, so this label does not depend on claiming that exchanging two chute actions changes their combined final result. Even difficulty 1 retains a coupled two-row target rather than independent direct vane toggles.
rationale.exploration_interface: The higher-profile inlet mapping is hidden until a mouth is inspected. D1 and D2 expose enough of the straight inlet segments that their mapping may be inferred statically, but the visible task still omits the consequential flip-after-routing rule. A first drop reveals that action effect before the remaining plan is chosen; it cannot itself complete the generated depth-two/depth-three target. Thus Exploration remains Yes in both modes at every difficulty, without claiming that the lower-profile mapping is fully hidden.

source_evidence.claim: Geometry consists of row/column gate indices and 2D center coordinates, with adjacent rows expanding by one gate. No depth coordinate participates in routing.
Current and target states are drawn as left/right rotated vanes on corresponding SVG lattices, with visible rails linking adjacent rows.

The inlet mapping is a permutation of all first-row columns. Planning in terms of entry columns therefore does not require retaining the full chute permutation; a selected column's physical chute can be inspected when needed.

The target and drop meter remain visible. An inlet trace stays visible while the mouth is hovered or focused, and simplified activation uses that same mouth. Repeated inspection can replace memory of earlier routes.

A drop computes its complete consequence from the current board, blocks further drops while busy, animates, then leaves every resulting gate orientation in place. Only the marble and path disappear. No intervention during transit is possible or required.

Success replays settled discrete chute actions and checks the target within the drop budget. It imposes no transit-observation, action-duration or timing condition. This corroborates the visible static-state solution rather than establishing a label by itself.
Each action routes according to existing vane states and flips every visited gate; target generation searches this state graph and selects a reachable target at the configured exact depth.

The independent exported verifier replays all cascades and requires equality of the whole target state before the finite tray budget is exceeded. It does not grade merely selected top gates or visual similarity.

The inlet cover is rendered after the static inlet lines. Hover/focus reveals one actual inlet route and leave/blur hides it; the baseline information can be obtained only through this additional inspection surface rather than from the target card.
The manifold cover is opaque; the inspection trace is initially invisible and becomes visible only when inspection activates it. The final marble path is hidden after settlement.

The baseline is D4/simplified. D1-D5 respectively configure 2/3/3/4/4 chutes, 2/2/3/3/4 rows, target depths 2/3/5/7/9 and drop budgets 4/5/7/10/12. Both surfaces preserve these decisions; they change activation from a mouth click to a feed-marble drag.

Full-mode dragging has a stationary release target and a spatial distance acceptance threshold. There is no minimum hold duration or continuing autonomous effect during the drag, so dragging alone does not establish a temporal exception.
D1/D2 static inlet segments extend below the cover, but the first drop reveals the undisclosed flip-after-routing effect shared by both input modes.
Target generation depends on flips and selects depth-two/depth-three targets in the first two profiles, which cannot be completed by the discovery drop alone.

limitations: Source-based classification; not an observed human or screenshot-only agent pass, and not an exhaustive proof over every conceivable solving policy.

baseline_description.interaction: Move the pointer over the water to position the inspection lens; press Space to photograph at that lens.
baseline_description.difficulty: Six target identities among nine look-alikes, full rotations and single-notch distinctions.

rationale.visual: Identity and species are encoded by a flat polygon's tail-lobe geometry and notch pattern. Pose changes are translation, rotation in the canvas plane, and uniform scale; no depth, occlusion in three dimensions, or 3D viewpoint reconstruction is involved.
rationale.temporal: D2-D5 have multiple individuals per species, reshuffle unmarked individuals after each successful photograph, and reject duplicate photographs. A normal screenshot-only solution must retain the photographed tail identities across the changed layouts. The usable enlarged inspection view does not retain a photographic identity ledger; the microscopic overview polygons are not a reliable basis for a general canonical ordering policy. D1 is separately No because there is only one individual per species and the visible photograph count and current lens species suffice.
rationale.reasoning_planning: At D4 there are three individuals of each listed species. Photographing one makes that same individual forbidden on every later layout even though it remains visible and unmarked; a duplicate or off-list selection immediately closes the attempt. The solution must enforce coverage without repetition by maintaining the selected set or a systematic identity ordering. This is a dependency between choices beyond merely recognizing a species.
rationale.exploration_interface: Aiming the lens reveals a species label and a three-times-enlarged tail crop. That interaction supplies the usable identity evidence needed to choose a photograph, rather than merely advancing to the next task state. The full pointer/Space surface and simplified coordinate/photograph controls preserve this information acquisition at all five difficulties.

configuration_exceptions.reason: D1 has exactly one animal of each species, so each of the two listed species identifies a unique target. Photograph the first listed species when the visible count is zero and the second when it is one. This reduces selection to species recognition and a simple visible progress sequence, without distinguishing competing individuals or planning an identity-coverage strategy.

source_evidence.claim: D1 sets animal_count to three with fixed orientation and scale.
The generator creates animal_count/3 individuals per species and lists two species, yielding one individual per listed species at D1.
The species list and current focus species are visible, the photograph count persists, and both modes use the same selection and coverage rules.

configuration_exceptions.reason: A general D1 procedure can use the current count to request the first, then second, listed species, reading the current lens species without recalling earlier individual identities. After aiming at the chosen animal, retry the shutter at the same coordinates if it has drifted out of the lens: empty shutters do nothing, the periodic animal returns, swept regions cannot admit a different animal, and a successful shutter clears the aim. This removes any need to infer motion, retain earlier selections, or time the action; the visible count alone determines the next target species.

source_evidence.claim: D1 creates one individual per species, and generated swept regions stay separated despite periodic drift.

The current count and list order are visible; inspection reports the focused species; empty shutters have no effect; successful shutters reset the aim; both input modes implement these same behaviors.
Species and individual notches determine a 2D polygon used both for complete animal rendering and tail crops.
Animals are translated, rotated in the canvas plane, and scaled; the inspection card draws a magnified crop with the same angle and scale.

The UI exposes a photograph total and no contact sheet; drawing does not mark selected animals. Each photograph changes the layout, clears the aim, and leaves the total count visible. The overview nevertheless continues to render every full identity polygon.

The generator separates complete swept bounding boxes and deranges identities between layouts. This prevents a stationary lens within one animal's swept region from accidentally targeting a different animal during the same epoch.

Motion is periodic within each layout. An empty-lens shutter does not record a photograph or end the attempt, and a successful shutter clears the aim. Thus movement cannot by itself prove that interpreting motion or timing a shutter is necessary.
D4 generates nine animals with three distinct notch patterns per species and selects all individuals of two species as required targets.

The replay requires the actual animal under the lens, rejects duplicate and off-list photographs, and accepts only exact complete coverage followed by submission. Earlier selection changes which later selections are allowed.

Aiming reveals the species label and enlarged tail, while the main view already draws the same unmasked identity geometry and the list shows species silhouettes. The two interaction modes change only how the lens and shutter are operated.

The overview and 280-by-220 inspection card are displayed together, but only one enlarged inspection is available. CSS scales the overview within the fixed-width workspace, making actual screenshot legibility material to whether lens inspection is necessary.
The exported verifier loads the exported transcript, truth, and public state and reruns the same independent geometry-and-coverage grader.
The lens reveals enlarged identity information; successful photos reshuffle unmarked individuals while duplicate identities are rejected.

baseline_description.interaction: Drag pane headers between slots, drag directly inside artwork to pan, wheel to zoom, and drag source fragments through the tray onto the visible torn opening; replay checks the physical hit regions, pointer traces, wheel direction, and drop pose.
baseline_description.difficulty: The unchanged source-selected configuration: all four pane transforms are displaced, all panes start out of place in a two- or three-swap derangement, every crossing reveals a source-derived fragment, and two same-family near-matches compete at 28-unit alignment tolerance.

rationale.visual: The necessary spatial problem is planar: identify illustrated contour segments, compare fragment line geometry, arrange a two-by-two set of panes, and match positions and scales across their edges. Pan, zoom, and fragment placement operate on x/y coordinates. Layer compositing and illustrated buildings do not require reconstructing three-dimensional geometry.
rationale.temporal: A solution can use successive static board states. The current pilgrim, current torn opening, current transforms, and previously peeled or stacked fragments remain represented visually. Crossing increments the stage immediately, briefly locks direct controls, and automatically ends its 520 ms animation; the solver need only wait for the next static state. Direct drags are evaluated by spatial traces and endpoints, with no minimum hold duration, velocity condition, or autonomous movement to track. The changing artwork during a pan follows pointer displacement, so planned short drags and inspection after release avoid time-extended control. Later fragments appearing after a crossing are a simple progression rather than required temporal memory.
rationale.reasoning_planning: The agent must infer which pictures form the route, choose swaps that put the source and target in the required adjacent slots, and choose coupled translation and scale adjustments that satisfy contour continuity. An intermediate picture participates in both an incoming and outgoing join, so its transform affects subsequent progress. A visually similar fragment is insufficient unless its line geometry matches the current opening, and it must be lifted before it can be placed. These are route and action-dependency constraints beyond identifying a pictured object. Across difficulties 1 through 5, the implementation retains at least one displaced transform and one required fragment; difficulty 1 removes slot-order search but still requires fitting the remaining transformed contour into the assembled route.
rationale.exploration_interface: The pictures are movable views with clipped content, not complete fixed diagrams: displaced contours and source fragments can lie outside the visible pane and must be exposed by panning or zooming. In full mode, the agent must also establish how the header, artwork, source fragment, tray, and opening participate in the manipulation sequence; the displayed task header gives only the destination goal, and a bound fragment cannot be dropped directly into an opening. The simplified controls expose the available fragments and make their lift/placement actions explicit, but retain the cropped, displaced picture views and the need to inspect the route through those views. This decision does not count the automatic appearance of later fragments, crossing feedback, or routine control activation as exploration by themselves. All five difficulty profiles and both input modes were examined; reduced scrambling, clutter, decoys, and alignment precision do not establish a supported capability-label exception.

source_evidence.claim: All route geometry uses two-dimensional points and a uniform scale plus x/y translation; three joins connect the fixed two-by-two route slots.
The visible fragment and opening expose line direction, crossbars, and hatching; the route is drawn as planar scene contours rather than as navigable 3D geometry.
The current stage is represented by the pilgrim and current target opening, while stacked fragments remain drawn in their current positions.
An accepted join advances the stage and starts a fixed automatic 520 ms crossing transition; no action must be chosen during that transition.

Pan movement derives directly from pointer displacement, and panel and fragment actions commit at the release endpoint. The interaction has no autonomous hold effect or duration-dependent success condition.
Pan and zoom replay checks spatial endpoints, bounds, detents, and selected input evidence rather than elapsed time or movement speed.
A crossing requires the correct source and target pane identities in specific slots, both contour transforms within tolerance, and the required fragment stacked on the correct target at a valid pose.
Moving a pane swaps another pane; pan and zoom persist on that pane; a fragment must transition from bound to peeled before placement. Those action effects constrain subsequent route assembly.

baseline_description.interaction: Drag labelled stars directly while watching the crossing count update.
baseline_description.difficulty: The baseline: a nine-star wheel (eight rim stars and a hub), three seeded swaps, and at least eight crossings.

rationale.visual: The necessary spatial information is planar: labelled vertex positions, which straight edges connect them, line intersections, coincident edge segments, and distances between stars. The renderer and grader use only x/y coordinates and planar segment geometry. The elliptical background guides and star imagery add no depth requirement.
rationale.temporal: A solution can choose each destination from a stationary drawing, execute an arbitrarily timed drag, and inspect the next stationary drawing. Positions change only in response to pointer events; holding still produces no continuing movement. The full-mode grader checks the drag's start and end coordinates and the existence of a matching pointer path, but it does not require a duration, speed, intermediate crossing-free route, or timed release. All task-relevant graph geometry and conflict counts persist in the current display, so earlier hidden state and motion interpretation are unnecessary. Simplified selection is visibly marked and also requires no temporal memory.
rationale.reasoning_planning: The UI does not supply target slots or a finished template. The agent must infer a crossing-free embedding of the fixed graph and choose vertex destinations whose multiple incident edges remain compatible with the other vertices' placements. Moving one star changes several segments and can remove some conflicts while creating others; resolving all of these simultaneous constraints requires more than recognizing a crossing. This remains true for the five-star cycle at difficulty 1, the wheel profiles at difficulties 2 and 3, and the double-ring profiles at difficulties 4 and 5.
rationale.exploration_interface: The instructions explicitly describe the active input surface and the objective. All stars and fixed edges are drawn from the start, and the UI continuously reports crossings, overlaps, and crowded stars. Moves update the same visible graph and its ordinary conflict feedback; there is no reveal control, hidden rule to discover, or information-gathering stage required before solving. Untangling may make overlapping lines easier to inspect, but changing the drawing is the stated puzzle operation and does not introduce a separate mandatory exploration requirement. The canonical solution coordinates are private, but they are not information the player needs: any valid embedding is accepted. Both input modes state their controls explicitly.
rationale.configuration_review: Examined all ten difficulty/interaction combinations. Difficulty 1 uses a five-star cycle; difficulties 2 and 3 use seven- and nine-star wheels; difficulties 4 and 5 use eleven- and fifteen-star double rings. The profiles vary topology, scrambling, minimum initial crossings, and minimum star separation. Both modes operate on the same generated graph and accept the same final geometric conditions. Full mode uses direct dragging, while simplified mode selects a star and then a destination. These differences do not support a change to any of the four baseline capability labels.

source_evidence.claim: The browser computes planar segment intersections, collinear edge overlaps, and Euclidean star separation, then draws every edge and labelled vertex on a 2D canvas with visible conflict counts.

Dragging directly assigns the pointer's current coordinates and records the final endpoint; simplified moves assign the clicked destination. There is no task motion or time integration between events, and the selected star remains visibly highlighted.

Replay validates event order, starting geometry, canvas bounds, and full-mode path endpoints, then checks the final embedding. It does not validate movement duration, speed, intermediate-path conflicts, or any timed target state.

The page explains dragging or select-then-click according to the selected mode, displays every fixed edge and labelled star, and provides persistent conflict counts and selected-star feedback. Movement implements the explained operation rather than revealing an undisclosed rule or separate hidden information source.

baseline_description.interaction: Left-drag road paths and home entrances; right-click segments to remove them.
baseline_description.difficulty: Three crossed flows and six eventual workshops require shared-network planning and expansion while carts return.

rationale.visual: The necessary spatial information is a flat orthogonal road graph: neighboring pins, legal river crossings, building obstacles, entrance directions, and matching colored/symbol-marked homes and workshops. The drawn roofs and cart rotation do not create any depth-dependent decision.
rationale.temporal: The town evolves after OPEN TOWN, but the required decisions can be made from persistent current information: active workshop symbols, queues, delivery totals, and the road graph. Cart movement, round trips, and the safe completion of an occupied road's closure are automatic. Newly opened workshops supply the next visible routing problem. Even a temporary prioritization edit can be conditioned on a displayed delivery count rather than elapsed time or hidden history. Road drags join fixed pins and have no required duration, and simplified clicks have the same effects. Growing queues impose urgency, but a deadline and routine state transitions alone do not establish the temporal capability under the supplied guideline.
rationale.reasoning_planning: The agent must construct a usable transport network under a finite road budget, route around blocked river cells and buildings, respect home entrances, and preserve outward and return connectivity. Shared segments admit only one cart at a time, and automatic nearest-route dispatch can let a primary workshop compete with its newly opened partner. Choosing shared routes, extensions, or temporary spur removal affects subsequent access and delivery service. Even the one-color profile still requires constructing and extending a route to a second workshop rather than merely recognizing a matching icon.
rationale.exploration_interface: The visible instructions explain the selected input surface, matching rule, round trips, segment occupancy, deferred road closure, and the two-delivery workshop opening rule. The map and current counters expose the information needed for routing. Initially fenced workshops reveal their lanterns automatically during required delivery progress; this is a transition to the next visible problem rather than an exploratory reveal action. No probing operation, hidden panel, or unknown control mapping is necessary. Observing ordinary route and queue feedback does not independently establish exploration.

source_evidence.claim: Generates an 11 by 7 planar graph with shuffled home/workshop rows, optional river bridge rows, fixed entrance neighbors, and a shared lantern palette.

The reference strategy chooses network changes from current active flags, delivery counts, entrances, and roads; it does not use cart velocity, elapsed travel time, or remembered earlier observations. This is supporting implementation evidence only: the solver reads internal state and is not screenshot-only gameplay verification. The corresponding active symbols, delivery counts, entrances, and roads are drawn in the UI.
